work.text: James McNeill Whistler created thinly painted compositions with flat, nearly abstract passages, purposefully subtle in character. He called works such as this one an “arrangement,” emphasizing formal elements rather than subject matter.

moment.text: The painting still serves as a portrait—it was commissioned by Chicago attorney Arthur Jerome Eddy, a collector and advocate of modern art. After seeing Whistler’s work at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in the city, Eddy traveled to the artist’s studio in Paris expressly to sit for this portrait.

source.author: Art Institute of Chicago
source.title: Arrangement in Flesh Color and Brown: Portrait of Arthur Jerome Eddy

moment.text: Whistler was not so successful a portrait painter as the other famous expatriate American John Singer Sargent.

matters.text: His description of Mr. Eddy was, “Well, you know, he is the only man who ever did get a picture out of me on time, while I worked and he waited!”

source.author: Elizabeth Robins Pennell and Joseph Pennell
source.title: The Life of James McNeill Whistler, vol. 2
source.publisher: William Heinemann / J. B. Lippincott (Internet Archive scan)

matters.text: The two became lasting friends, and Eddy published a book on Whistler after the artist’s death in 1903.
